nameStory: The 'straw' in straw foxglove refers to its pale, straw-colored yellow flowers that are much lighter than the bright yellows of other foxgloves. Like all foxgloves, the tubular flowers were thought to resemble the fingers of a glove, giving the entire genus its 'foxglove' name.
description: Straw foxglove is a tall perennial herb that produces elegant spikes of small, pale yellow tubular flowers. This European native grows 2-4 feet tall with a slender, upright habit. The plant forms a basal rosette of leaves with flower spikes rising above, creating a graceful vertical accent in the garden.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers in pale straw-yellow, arranged in a tall, narrow spike along one side of the stem. Each flower is about half an inch long with a slightly flared opening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and somewhat leathery. Lower leaves form a rosette at the base, while upper leaves alternate up the stem and are progressively smaller.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright perennial 2-4 feet tall with a slender profile. Multiple flower spikes may emerge from a single plant, creating a clustered appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small brown capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny seeds. The dried seed pods often persist on the spike well into fall.

habitat: In New England, straw foxglove is primarily found as an escaped garden plant in disturbed areas, woodland edges, and along roadsides. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate partial shade to full sun conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as a basal rosette of narrow green leaves. Flower spikes begin developing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer with tall spikes of pale yellow flowers. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, turning brown and splitting open. The plant begins to die back to its basal rosette.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, with only the root system surviving underground until spring regrowth.

funFact: Despite being the most subtle-looking foxglove, straw foxglove contains the same heart-affecting compounds as its showier purple cousin - compounds that led to the development of the heart medication digitalis!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other yellow foxgloves, but straw foxglove has the palest, most cream-colored flowers of the group. Remember: 'straw' means pale and subtle, not bright yellow like fresh corn.
contextualKnowledge: All foxgloves, including this seemingly innocent pale species, are highly toxic if eaten. They contain powerful cardiac glycosides that affect heart function. Always admire from a distance and wash hands after handling.
compareHints: Among foxgloves in New England, straw foxglove is distinguished by its pale, cream-yellow flowers that are much smaller and more numerous than the large, bright yellow blooms of yellow foxglove (Digitalis grandiflora). Purple foxglove is easy to distinguish by its purple-pink flowers, while straw foxglove maintains its subtle, understated appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple foxglove is the most common foxglove species in New England and the most likely to naturalize from gardens.
Yellow foxglove stands out from its more common cousin, purple foxglove, by its soft yellow color and larger individual blooms.
Woolly foxglove stands out from other foxgloves by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves and small, densely-packed cream flowers.
Among the foxglove family, Rusty Foxglove is unique for its rust-brown flowers - Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms, while Yellow Foxglove (rarely seen here) has pale yellow flowers.
